items.scenario: You ask Claude to 'summarise the requirements' from a 30-message client thread. The summary lists 'SSO via Okta' as a requirement, but nobody can remember it being said.
items.question: How should you restructure the extraction?
options: Ask Claude to be more careful and regenerate the summary from the same thread
Require a verbatim source quote per requirement, with inferences listed as assumptions
Switch to the highest effort setting so it reasons harder about what the client meant
Remove all requirements that sound technical, since a business client wouldn't write them
items.explanation: Requiring a quote per row turns generation into retrieval plus labelling, and makes fabrication checkable: search the source for the quote.
distractors: An exhortation doesn't change the task. Plausible inventions remain.
More reasoning doesn't make the output traceable.
Technical-sounding requirements can be real. The problem is traceability.

items.scenario: Extracted requirements for a payments feature contain functional requirements only. The client's emails never mention performance, availability or data residency.
items.question: What should you do about the missing non-functional requirements?
options: Record 'NFRs: none' in the spec, since the client did not state any in the thread
Fill in reasonable industry-standard NFRs and include them in the spec as requirements
Treat it as a gap: probe each NFR category and add questions with defaults to the client list
Defer NFRs until after go-live, when real production load and usage are actually known
items.explanation: Clients rarely state NFRs. Silence is a gap, not a 'none'. Ask, and make your defaults visible.
distractors: Silence isn't confirmation. Discovering residency or latency needs late is expensive.
Invented values presented as requirements are fabrications. Label them as defaults or assumptions.
Performance and residency can change the architecture. Deferring them is costly.

items.scenario: A generated story reads: 'As a system, I want an invoices_export table with a status column so that exports are tracked.'
items.question: Which INVEST problems does it show most clearly?
options: It is not Independent of other stories, and not Small enough for one sprint
Not Valuable to a named user, and not Negotiable: it prescribes the implementation
It is not Estimable, because a database table design cannot be sized in points
It has no problems, because it is specific, testable and clear about exactly what to build
items.explanation: 'As a system' names no user who gets value, and specifying the table fixes the design instead of stating the need.
distractors: Nothing in it suggests dependency or excessive size. The clear defects are value and negotiability.
A table can be estimated. The issue is that it's implementation, not need.
Specificity about implementation is the defect, not a virtue.

items.scenario: Your invoice export API is at v1 and used by external integrators. A new story makes the optional 'from' date in ExportRequest required, and Claude's change summary labels this 'additive: tightens validation'.
items.question: How should you classify and ship this change?
options: Additive, since no field is removed or renamed and the response shape is unchanged
Breaking: requests omitting 'from' now fail, so ship it in a new version with a deprecation window
Additive, as long as the changelog announces the new rule well before the next scheduled release
Not a contract change at all, because validation rules sit outside the OpenAPI schema itself
items.explanation: Tightening validation (optional to required, narrower enums, shorter limits) rejects requests that worked yesterday, so it is breaking. Classify against your written versioning rules, verify Claude's label rather than trusting it, and ship breaking changes under a new version with a deprecation window.
distractors: Removal and renaming aren't the only breaking changes. Clients that omit the field start getting errors.
A changelog informs clients but doesn't stop their existing requests failing on the day you ship.
The 'required' list and constraints are part of the OpenAPI schema. Changing them changes what clients must send.

items.scenario: A .NET team and a TypeScript team each asked Claude for 'the invoice API' and got different field casing and error shapes.
items.question: What fixes this at the source?
options: Let each team keep its own version of the contract and translate the names in the frontend
Agree one convention and one source-of-truth OpenAPI file, review against it, record an ADR
Ask Claude to merge both specs into one, choosing whichever naming looks better in each case
Switch to GraphQL, since it has no naming conventions for the two teams to disagree on
items.explanation: Claude follows the conventions it's given. One reviewed contract plus a recorded convention removes the two dialects.
distractors: Translation layers lock the inconsistency in.
'Whichever looks better' delegates a convention decision without criteria.
GraphQL schemas have naming conventions too. Switching tools doesn't decide the convention.

items.scenario: Claude drafts an ADR choosing a message queue. It states that 'Service X guarantees exactly-once delivery' and quotes a specific free-tier limit.
items.question: What must happen before the ADR is accepted?
options: Nothing extra, since ADRs record the team's opinions and trade-offs rather than facts
Check each factual claim against official vendor docs and cite it; named people decide
Ask Claude to add 'to the best of my knowledge' to each claim it cannot fully confirm
Remove the context section, so the ADR contains no factual claims that could turn out wrong
items.explanation: Guarantees and limits are high-risk, volatile claims. Verify and cite them. The decision itself is made by named humans.
distractors: ADRs record decisions built on factual premises, and false premises mean bad decisions.
A hedge doesn't verify anything.
Context is a required part of an ADR. Remove false claims, not context.

items.scenario: Sales asks for 'just a rough number' for a feature. Claude produces '12 developer-days' from the story list.
items.question: How should the estimate be delivered?
options: Send 12 days, since the client only asked for a rough number and will expect revisions
A range with stated assumptions and risks, owned by a named tech lead, marked indicative
Pad it by 50% to cover unknowns and send that figure without further explanation
Refuse to estimate until the full design is complete and every single requirement is signed off
items.explanation: Estimates go out assumption-tagged and with a named human owner. Claude knows nothing of your team's velocity and isn't accountable.
distractors: A single unowned number tends to become a commitment, for example in a fixed-price contract.
Hidden padding hides the assumptions instead of stating them.
An indicative, assumption-tagged range is the responsible answer. Refusing helps nobody.

items.scenario: Your team keeps architecture diagrams as PNG exports in a shared drive. They no longer match the ADRs or the API contract.
items.question: What change best addresses this?
options: Ask Claude to redraw the PNGs from the current code each quarter so they stay accurate
Keep diagrams as Mermaid or PlantUML text in the repo, reviewed with the ADR and contract
Stop drawing diagrams and rely on the code, which is always the real source of truth
Add a 'last updated' date to each PNG so readers know how far to trust it
items.explanation: Diagrams as code can be diffed and reviewed in the same change as the design they describe, which keeps them in sync.
distractors: Periodic redraws still drift between redraws and can't be reviewed as diffs.
Diagrams communicate design quickly. Dropping them loses that.
A date shows the drift but doesn't prevent it.

items.scenario: Asked for an architecture for an internal tool used by 40 people, Claude proposes microservices, event sourcing and Kubernetes. The team is three developers who know a single web framework well.
items.question: What is the best way to correct the design?
options: Accept it, since it follows published best practice from large, well-known engineering organisations
Give Claude the real constraints (team, load, budget) and ask for the simplest design that fits
Ask Claude to add a service mesh so the team gets observability across all the services
Pick the option with the most components, so the system can scale later without a rewrite
items.explanation: Claude drifts toward over-represented 'big' architectures. Real constraints and a 'simplest that meets the NFRs' framing reverse that bias. Team skill is a design constraint.
distractors: Published reference designs target very different scale and teams.
This adds complexity the team can't operate.
Scaling for unneeded load costs operating effort now for no benefit.

items.scenario: Mid-sprint, the client changes 'export within 1 minute' to 'export available in under 5 seconds'. You have requirement IDs, stories, an OpenAPI contract, an ADR and tests linked by references.
items.question: How should you assess the change's impact?
options: Regenerate all the artefacts from scratch so the new requirement is reflected everywhere at once
Trace forward from the changed NFR to each story, contract operation, ADR and test that cites it
Update only the requirement text, since the downstream artefacts will catch up in review
Ask Claude whether the change is small or large, then plan the follow-up work from that
items.explanation: Traceability makes impact analysis mechanical. Follow the references from the changed requirement to everything built on it, here including the async-queue ADR.
distractors: Regenerating throws away reviewed work and hides what actually changed.
Leaving the downstream artefacts unchanged leaves the ADR and contract wrong.
A size judgement without the trace is a guess.
